title: Parabolic Short
teaches: The parabolic short as we trade it: a stock that has already run far goes vertical for 3 to 5 days, gaps up on the climax day on record volume, and is shorted at market only after it cracks back under VWAP; the stop sits a few cents over the day's high, the size comes from that wide stop, the target is the daily 9 EMA within a few sessions, and a reclaim of the high, a passed window or a squeeze through the 2R gap ceiling ends it.

facts.claim: Bracco's fourth box: two days of rising volume.

questions.q: A red-hot stock has gone vertical for days and gaps up again this morning. What trade are we hunting here?
choices: Short it once it cracks
Short the gap right at the open
Buy the gap, it's the strongest name
Nothing, never short a leader
questions.why: Short it once it cracks. That's the parabolic short. The burst is a 3-5 day move, the last vertical leg of a big run. We never short the climb itself. We wait for the crack, the break back under VWAP, and short that. It's a mean-reversion trade: a stretched stock snapping back. Sometimes it marks a lasting top, not always. One more thing. I only recommend shorting to traders who have already made $1 million trading.
questions.lesson_line: Let it go vertical. Short the crack, never the climb.

wrong.Short the gap right at the open: That's shorting into strength at the highs. The gap can keep running, and you're the one who gets run over.
wrong.Buy the gap, it's the strongest name: That's chasing the last leg. The stock is as stretched as it gets, right where it tends to snap back.
wrong.Nothing, never short a leader: Leaders going parabolic is exactly where this trade lives. A cycle often ends with the best names blowing off.

questions.simple: We short a stock that went vertical, but only once it cracks, never while it's still climbing.

reasons: defines the setup by the owner's house definition (B26)

questions.q: We don't short stocks above their 200-day, with one exception. Which short can you take up there?
choices: A parabolic short off a climax
Any short once it's up 50%
Any short when the market's Red
A short at a big round number
questions.answer: A parabolic short off a climax
questions.why: A parabolic short off a climax. Above the 200-day, that's the one short we take. Everything else up there is a stock in an uptrend, and shorting uptrends is how you get run over. The parabolic one is different. It's one of the hottest stocks in the market, far above its 200-day, and it just blew off in a burst. A big percent gain alone doesn't open that door. Neither does the market reading or a round number.
questions.lesson_line: Above the 200-day there's one short we take: the parabolic one.

wrong.Any short once it's up 50%: A percent gain isn't the test. Plenty of strong stocks are up 50% and still trending. Only the parabolic climax qualifies.
wrong.Any short when the market's Red: Red on our market filter means we're mostly in cash. It doesn't change where the stock sits against its 200-day.
wrong.A short at a big round number: Round numbers are where climax points often come. That's a cue, not a pass to short above the 200-day.

questions.simple: Above the 200-day we only short a parabolic climax. Nothing else gets us short up there.

reasons: one cited fact only (B26, h01) carries the key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
the exception test is held (D-040); the key uses only B26's own words

questions.q: We need a gap up on the climax day before we'll short it.
questions.why: True. No gap up, no trade. Bracco won't short without that gap-up, and neither do we. The gap is the exhaustion, the run spending its last buyers at the open. Any open above the prior close counts. A gap of 5% or more is the stronger one. Without the gap, a red day is just a red day.
questions.lesson_line: No gap up, no climax-day short.
questions.simple: True. The gap up is the run's last rush of buyers, so without it there's nothing to short.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook and the criteria card (the climax gap is settled there; the owner may loosen it)

questions.q: You're short the crack on a climax day. Where are you looking to cover?
questions.sentence: I cover a parabolic short at the daily ___ EMA.
questions.why: 9. The daily 9 EMA is the target. A stock stretched this far gets pulled back toward it like a magnet. That snap back is the trade. Before you short, find the 9 EMA and count how far away it is in R. If it's close, the trade is small. The longer averages are way too far off to plan around.
questions.lesson_line: The 9 EMA is the target. Know where it sits before you short.
questions.simple: The daily 9 EMA. A stretched stock snaps back toward it, so that's where you cover.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D47) plus Bracco's post
how much comes off at the 9 EMA is held (D-013); the key is the level only

questions.q: You just shorted the VWAP break on a climax day. Where does your stop go?
choices: Just over the high of the day
Just under the low of the day
At the 9 EMA, under price
A flat 3% above your entry
questions.answer: Just over the high of the day
questions.why: Just over the high of the day. The whole idea is that the top is in. If price gets back over that high, the top wasn't in and you're wrong. So the stop goes a few cents over it. It's a level on the chart, not a percent you picked. Then the size comes from that stop.
questions.lesson_line: The stop lives over the high. Lose that and the top wasn't in.

wrong.Just under the low of the day: That's a long's stop. On a short your risk is price going up, so the stop sits above.
wrong.At the 9 EMA, under price: The 9 EMA is where you cover. It's below price, so it can't be the stop on a short.
wrong.A flat 3% above your entry: The stop goes where the chart says you're wrong, the high of the day. A percent you pick ignores the chart.

questions.simple: Over the high of the day. If price gets back above it, the top wasn't in.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D47) and the criteria card (settled stop)

questions.q: On the climax day, you short the gap right at the open.
questions.why: False. Nothing at the open. A climax gap can keep running, and shorting the highs is how you get run over. Let it set the high first. The trade is the break back under VWAP, often 10 to 60 minutes in. That's when you know sellers have finally shown up.
questions.lesson_line: The open is for watching. The crack is for shorting.
questions.simple: False, we let it set the high and wait for the break under VWAP. Shorting the open is shorting strength.

reasons: rests on the card's proposed open-wait rule

questions.q: A stock has been running hard. Which of these makes it look more like a parabolic burst?
choices: Two straight overnight gap ups
A close back under the 50-day
Volume drying up the last two days
A ten-week base right before
questions.why: Two straight overnight gap ups. That's one of the boxes we check on a burst. The others: three straight up days, and two of three days with a bigger percent gain than the day before. Then two days of rising volume, and a gap up on the climax day. You don't need every box. The more you check, the stronger the setup.
questions.lesson_line: Count the boxes: up days, gap ups, bigger gains, rising volume, the climax gap.

wrong.A close back under the 50-day: A burst runs far above its averages. A close under the 50-day is a stock breaking down, not blowing off.
wrong.Volume drying up the last two days: In a burst we want volume rising, each day bigger than the last. Drying up is what we like in a base.
wrong.A ten-week base right before: A base is where a run starts. The boxes count the last few days, where it goes vertical.

questions.simple: Two straight gap ups. A burst is fast and speeding up, and back-to-back gaps show buyers paying up.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26's box list)
the count of boxes needed is held (D-040); only the boxes themselves are keyed

questions.q: The climax day gaps up and runs for 20 minutes, then rolls over. Where's your first entry?
choices: The break back under VWAP
The first print at the open
The first green 5-minute bar
A daily close under the 9 EMA
questions.why: The break back under VWAP. Bracco calls this shape the U-Turn: it runs early, then sellers show up 10 to 60 minutes in. He never enters before price at least breaks VWAP, and neither do we. Under VWAP, the average buyer today is losing money. Those gap chasers are trapped, and that's your edge. Send the market order on the break, stop over the high of the day.
questions.lesson_line: First entry: the VWAP break after the high is in.

wrong.The first green 5-minute bar: A green bar is buyers still pushing. You want the break down, not a bounce.
wrong.A daily close under the 9 EMA: The 9 EMA is where you cover. By the time it closes under it, the trade's already done.
wrong.The first print at the open: The high isn't set yet at the open. Short there and you're guessing at the top.

questions.simple: Short the break under VWAP. That's when the gap buyers are trapped and sellers have taken over.

reasons: the card's VWAP trigger is a proposed rule (ps.vwap_trigger)
several agreeing quotes

questions.q: On a daily chart, a climax day that closes green is the crack.
questions.why: False. On a daily chart the crack is a close under the open: it opens higher and closes lower. A green close means buyers held it all day. Shorting a green climax day won 23% of the time. The real trigger is the VWAP break during the day. The red daily bar is just how that looks afterward.
questions.lesson_line: Opens higher, closes lower. That's the crack on a daily chart.
questions.simple: False, the crack on a daily chart is a red close under the open. Green means buyers still won the day.

reasons: the 23% is a result from our own scan
rests on the card's daily-bar stand-in

questions.q: Tap the days that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: Bracco's parabolic burst, the final leg of a run, usually lasts ___ days.
questions.why: 3 to 5. Bracco: the parabolic burst is a 3-5 day move that marks the final leg. In his studies most bursts last 3 to 5 days. Kullamagi also wants the stock up 3 to 5 or more days in a row. Most is not all. The run before the burst can be longer, as in GDS, a 13-session run.
questions.lesson_line: A burst is short, about 3 to 5 days, and the climax gap comes late in it.
questions.simple: A burst lasts about 3 to 5 days, and it is only the last leg of a longer run.

reasons: a stable definition with agreeing quotes from two publishers

questions.q: Kullamagi's rule of thumb for a larger-cap parabolic short: how far has the stock already run?
choices: 50% to 100%+ in days or weeks
10% to 20% over a few months
300% to 1,000%+ in days or weeks
Doesn't matter, only the gap
questions.why: 50% to 100% or more, in days or weeks. That's Kullamagi's bar for a larger cap. For a smaller cap he wants 300% to 1,000% or more. Think of the run as the ticket in. A stock has to be stretched before there's anything to snap back. But the percent alone isn't the test. Bracco calls judging by percent gain alone a frequent mistake. The shape has to be vertical too.
questions.lesson_line: Big run first. Then look at the shape.

wrong.10% to 20% over a few months: That's a normal move. Nothing is stretched enough to snap back.
wrong.300% to 1,000%+ in days or weeks: That's his bar for a smaller cap, not a larger one.
wrong.Doesn't matter, only the gap: The gap ends a run. Without a big run first, there's nothing for it to exhaust.

questions.simple: A larger cap needs to be up a lot, fast. Without a big run first, there's nothing to snap back.

reasons: the cap bands are one author's rule (Kullamagi) plus the card's proposed floor
small-cap bands are held (D-122); only the larger-cap floor is keyed

questions.q: Can you short this one?
choices: No, the run's too young
Yes, gap up and a red close
Yes, the gap is the trigger
No, the gap is under 5%
questions.why: No. Pass on this one. It's three days out of a six-month base. That's a fresh breakout, not a tired run. Bracco calls a short like that very short lived at best. RGTI was this case: fresh out of a base, it made a new high on day 6 and took the stop. The candle looks right. The context is wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Right candle, wrong week. A fresh breakout isn't a climax.

wrong.Yes, gap up and a red close: The daily bar fits, the context doesn't. Three days out of a base, there's no exhausted run to short.
wrong.Yes, the gap is the trigger: The gap sets it up and the VWAP break triggers it. A stock this fresh has no setup anyway.
wrong.No, the gap is under 5%: 5% or more is the stronger gap, not a minimum. Any gap up passes. The young run is the problem.

questions.story: Three days ago this stock broke out of a six-month base. Two up days. Today it gaps up 4% and closes red.
questions.simple: No, it just broke out of a long base. A fresh breakout isn't a tired run, so there's nothing to fade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26) and the card's not-this-setup list

questions.q: A climax short you can't borrow at a fair fee is a pass, however good the chart looks.
questions.why: True. Pass. If the stock is hard to borrow or the fee is high, we skip it. Squeeze names are often hard to borrow, and a high fee eats into the trade before it even moves. Check the borrow with your broker before the climax day, not at the trigger.
questions.lesson_line: No borrow, no trade.
questions.simple: True, no borrow at a fair fee means no trade. The chart doesn't pay the fee.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (D48)

questions.q: The VWAP break prints on the climax day. What order do you send?
choices: A market order, right now
A limit a few cents lower
A sell-stop under the day's low
Wait for the 5-minute bar to close
questions.why: A market order, right now. The trigger printed and your stop is already known, a few cents over the high of the day. There's nothing left to wait for. A limit order can leave you watching it fall without you. The sell-stop under the day's low is Bracco's second entry. We don't take it. One entry, full size, one stop.
questions.lesson_line: Trigger prints, you're in at market.

wrong.A sell-stop under the day's low: That's Bracco's second entry, at the break of the day's low. We take one entry, at the VWAP break.
wrong.Wait for the 5-minute bar to close: The trigger is the break, not a bar close. Waiting just gives you a worse fill and a wider stop.
wrong.A limit a few cents lower: You might never get filled. On a fast crack, price can be gone before it comes back to your limit.

questions.simple: A market order the moment it breaks. The stop is known, so waiting only costs you a worse fill.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, one entry, settled)

questions.q: It's through your stop by a few cents. What do you do?
choices: Out, the high is reclaimed
Hold, it's only a few cents
Move the stop up to 54.00
Add, the top is still in
questions.why: Out. It's 52.60, through your 52.56 stop. Price is back over the high of the day, so the top wasn't in, or your timing was off. Either way you're flat. The stop is the exit, and it never moves wider. Don't add either. Parabolic runs go further than anyone thinks, and adding turns a small loss into a big one.
questions.lesson_line: Over the high, you're wrong. Wrong is flat.

wrong.Hold, it's only a few cents: A few cents over the high is over the high. A new high says the top wasn't in.
wrong.Move the stop up to 54.00: Widening the stop turns a planned loss into an open-ended one. It never moves wider.
wrong.Add, the top is still in: Adding to a losing short is the named mistake. Bracco never adds when he's down, and neither do we.

questions.story: You shorted the VWAP break at 48.50. Your stop is 52.56, a few cents over the high of the day. At 2 pm it trades 52.60.
questions.simple: Get out. Price is back over the high of the day, so the top wasn't in.

deeper.example: A reclaim can come after a long wait. PLUG's climax was 2021-01-13. A marginal higher high eight sessions later took the stop, and the real top came on 2021-01-26. Out is still out, even when the stock then turns.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop never widens; settled)

questions.q: Check the volume on that last bar. What do you want to see there?
choices: The biggest volume of the run
Lighter than the day before
Average, volume doesn't matter
Heavy only in the last hour

TIGR printed 1.56x the highest volume of its prior 20 sessions here. It raises the grade. It's a tell, though, not the trigger. You still wait for the VWAP break.

wrong.No, a stop-out ends the idea: One stop-out doesn't close it. Two failed triggers, or the window passing, does.

When it falls 50% from the high
When it closes under the 200-day
The next morning, whatever happens

Yes; the gap is the trigger
Yes; a small starter short here

questions.lesson_line: The crowd screaming top is not a trigger. The VWAP break is.

wrong.Yes; the gap is the trigger: The gap is the setup. The trigger is the break under VWAP after the high is set.

choices: 53.40, the first 30-minute high
52.70, the first 30-minute low
Still 52.56, the stop is the stop
Out now, it's past 2R
questions.why: 53.40, the high of that first 30-minute bar. A gap through your stop is the one time the stop can move. The first 30 minutes decide, and on a short the new stop is that bar's high. questions.lesson_line: A gap through the stop: the first 30 minutes decide.

wrong.52.70, the first 30-minute low: The bar's low is the long-side version. On a short the risk is up, so it's the high.

questions.q: When the stock breaks the day's low, we add a second short to the position.
questions.why: False. One entry, full size, one stop. That's the whole position. Bracco takes a second short when it breaks the day's lows. We don't plan one. A rare add to a winner is a feel call, never the plan. Adding later means a bigger position under the same stop over the high, so a squeeze hurts more. Pick your spot at the VWAP break and size it right there.
questions.lesson_line: One entry, one stop, full size.
questions.simple: False, we short once, full size, with one stop. Adding later only makes a squeeze hurt more.

reasons: rests on the owner's one-entry rule (A5)

Yes, the crack is real
Yes, the stop's still over the high
No, shorts belong at the high
questions.answer: No, it's too far past the break
questions.why: No. 47.50 is more than 4% under the 50.00 break. We never chase more than 4% past a trigger, and on a short that's mirrored. Chase it and your stop stays up over the high, so it's wider and you get fewer shares for the same risk. Worse fill, worse trade. I'd rather miss it than chase it.
questions.lesson_line: I'd rather miss it than chase it. 4% and done, both ways.

wrong.Yes, the crack is real: Real and clean doesn't make it a good entry. Past 4%, you're chasing.
wrong.Yes, the stop's still over the high: That's the problem. The stop's still up there, so it's wider and your size shrinks.

questions.simple: No, it's already more than 4 percent under the break. Chasing means a wider stop and fewer shares.

deeper.trap: A clean crack is not a free pass. The 4% line is about price, not about how good the chart looks. A late fill keeps the same stop over the high, so the stop is wider and the share count smaller. Miss it and wait for the next idea.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: In a parabolic run the pauses get ___ as the price goes higher.
questions.why: Shorter. Bracco: ideally the consolidation periods shorten as the price surges higher, with minimal pullbacks. Our card adds the ATR rising, and a measurable form: the last 2 to 3 weekly ranges each larger than the one before. A steady linear climb does not do this, and Bracco says to avoid it.
questions.lesson_line: Parabolic means the pauses get shorter. Linear means they do not.
questions.simple: In a parabolic run the pauses get shorter and the pullbacks smaller as price climbs.

deeper.counter: A stock can be up a lot and still be linear. Percent gain alone does not make a run parabolic. Bracco calls judging by percent gain alone a frequent mistake.

Yes; the burst must be done
Yes; tomorrow will gap down

questions.lesson_line: A green climax day has not cracked. Strength is not a trigger.

wrong.Yes; the burst must be done: Nobody knows the burst is done until it cracks. Green at the close means it has not.

questions.q: Two climax days. One has four boxes, a 15% gap and record volume. The other: two boxes, a 2% gap, average volume. Which do you want?
choices: The four-box day, by a mile
The two-box day, it's quieter
Either, only the crack counts
Neither, only percent gain counts

questions.lesson_line: More boxes, bigger gap, record crowd: that's the stronger climax.

wrong.The two-box day, it's quieter: Quiet isn't safe here. Fewer boxes means less proof the run is done.
wrong.Either, only the crack counts: The crack is the trigger. The boxes, the gap and the volume tell you how good the setup is.
wrong.Neither, only percent gain counts: Bracco calls judging by percent gain alone a frequent mistake. The boxes tell you more.

The U-Turn, a run then a VWAP break
Quick Opening Range Breakdown
The second short at the day's low

the failed-bounce entry is Kullamagi's

questions.q: Same red candle as a climax. What setup is this?
choices: A News Failure, not a burst
A Parabolic Short on the gap
A Wedge Drop off the top
A Parabolic Long on the gap
questions.answer: A News Failure, not a burst
questions.why: A News Failure. A good-news gap up that closes red, with no burst before it. The candle looks like a climax. The days before it don't. A parabolic short needs the 3-5 day burst first, the run going vertical into the gap. This one had 2 of 4 boxes, no three straight up closes and no acceleration. AAOI was this exact case. Look left before you name the candle.
questions.lesson_line: Same candle, different setup. Look at the days before the gap.

wrong.A Parabolic Short on the gap: No burst, no parabola. A slow drift before the gap is the giveaway.
wrong.A Wedge Drop off the top: A Wedge Drop comes days after a top, sitting on the averages under the 200-day. This one's a gap up out of a drift.
wrong.A Parabolic Long on the gap: A Parabolic Long is a burst down into a gap down. This gapped up.

questions.story: This stock drifted up slowly for weeks. Today it gaps up 27.7% on a surprise headline and closes red. No three straight up days before it, no speed-up.
questions.simple: A News Failure. It drifted up slowly, then gapped on a headline and closed red, with no burst before it.

deeper.trap: The candle looks the same: a big gap up that closes red. The difference is the days before it. A Parabolic Short needs the burst first. A one-day 27.7% gap after a slow rise is the News Failure shape, which needs no burst.

reasons: figures come from our own scan

questions.q: Do those weekly ranges say parabolic?
choices: No, the middle week shrank
Yes, the red close is the crack
Yes, three big weeks of range
No, it's above its 200-day
questions.why: No. In a parabolic run each week's range is bigger than the one before. Here it went 12.33, then 5.27, then 13.33. The middle week shrank, so it's a bumpy climb, not one that's speeding up. Bracco calls back-to-back weeks of range expansion extremely important. This was a steady leader having one bad day. NVDA gave 1.19R before the stop. The 200-day isn't the test, since a parabolic short can sit above it.
questions.lesson_line: A leader's one bad day isn't a climax. The weeks before it decide.

wrong.Yes, the red close is the crack: The crack only matters on a parabolic run. This run was linear.
wrong.Yes, three big weeks of range: Big isn't the test. Each week has to be bigger than the last, and the middle one shrank.
wrong.No, it's above its 200-day: A parabolic short is the one short we take above the 200-day. The shrinking week is what rules it out.

questions.story: A strong leader at highs. Its last three weekly ranges were 12.33, 5.27 and 13.33 points. Today it gaps up and closes red.
questions.simple: No, the middle week's range shrank, so the climb wasn't speeding up. One bad day at highs isn't a climax.

deeper.trap: A single big red day at highs looks like a climax. The weeks before it decide. Two big weeks around one small week is a bumpy climb, not an accelerating one. Bracco warns that judging by percent gain alone, without the structure, is a frequent mistake.

reasons: rests on the card's weekly-range form
figures come from our own scan

questions.q: An index ETF drops four days straight in a burst, gaps down on day 5, then turns up during the day. Which trade is it?
choices: The Parabolic Long, on the turn
The Parabolic Short, on the crack
A Wedge Drop on the gap down
No trade, it's below the 200-day
questions.answer: The Parabolic Long, on the turn
questions.why: The Parabolic Long. It's the short flipped: a burst down, a gap down on the climax day, bought on the turn during the day. The stop goes under the low of the day, and the 9 EMA above is the target. Everything flips. One catch on the 200-day. Below it, stocks are a hard no. Only an index or a levered ETF gets this exception.
questions.lesson_line: Check which way the burst went. Down means the long, with everything flipped.

wrong.The Parabolic Short, on the crack: A short needs a burst up and a gap up. This burst ran down.
wrong.A Wedge Drop on the gap down: A Wedge Drop is a stall at the averages after a top, then a break lower. This one's a fast burst down.
wrong.No trade, it's below the 200-day: On an index or a levered ETF we can buy a parabolic long under the 200-day. On a single stock it's a hard no.

questions.simple: The Parabolic Long, the short flipped. A burst down into a gap down, bought when it turns up.

reasons: rests on the owner's mirror rule (B26)

questions.q: It's a short, but which one?
choices: A Wedge Drop on the break
A Parabolic Short on the break
A Parabolic Long on the break
A News Failure on the break
questions.answer: A Wedge Drop on the break
questions.why: A Wedge Drop. It comes days after the top, from a stall at the 9 EMA, and only under the 200-day. A parabolic short is a different animal. It happens on the climax day itself, with the stock stretched far above its averages. This one's sitting right on them. Check two things: the distance from the averages, and which side of the 200-day it's on.
questions.lesson_line: The climax is far from the averages. The Wedge Drop sits on them.

wrong.A Parabolic Short on the break: The climax day is far above the averages. This stock is sitting on them, days after its top.
wrong.A Parabolic Long on the break: A long needs a burst down and a gap down. This one's a stall after a top.
wrong.A News Failure on the break: A News Failure is a good-news gap up that closes red. There was no gap here, just a stall and a break.

questions.story: A stock under its 200-day topped days ago, then stalled five days at its 9 EMA. Today it broke down out of that stall.
questions.simple: A Wedge Drop. It's a stall at the 9 EMA days after the top, under the 200-day, then a break down.

deeper.trap: Both are shorts, so the names are easy to mix up. Check how far the price is from its averages, and which side of the 200-day it's on. Far above on the climax day is the Parabolic Short. On the averages, days later, under the 200-day, is the Wedge Drop.

reasons: rests on the card's setup definitions

questions.q: Short 521.70, stop 565.54, the 9 EMA at 455.00. How many R do you make covering at the 9 EMA?
questions.why: 1.52R. Your risk is the stop minus your entry: 565.54 minus 521.70 is 43.84 a share. Your gain is the entry minus the 9 EMA: 521.70 minus 455.00 is 66.70. 66.70 over 43.84 is 1.52R. Do this before you short, so you know what the trade can pay against what it risks. The entry and stop are CGC's. That stop sat 8.4% away, wider than I like. The 9 EMA level is made up for the drill.
questions.lesson_line: Count the 9 EMA in R before you short.
questions.simple: 1.52R. The gain to the 9 EMA divided by the risk to your stop.

reasons: a computed key (R multiple)
how much comes off at the 9 EMA is held (D-013); only the arithmetic is keyed

wrong.2.52R: You measured from the stop, not your entry.
wrong.11.90R: You divided your entry price by R. Divide the gain by R.

questions.q: When the honest stop over the climax high is more than 5% away, we mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.why: True. We want the stop 1-3% away, 3.5% is good, and up to 5% we accept. The climax high is often further than that. In our daily-bar examples GDS was 8.4%, BILI 7.2% and TPL 8.9% away. Past 5%, I mostly wait for a tighter trigger. And never pull the stop in just to make the size fit. The stop goes where the chart says you're wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Never pick a size first and back-fit the stop.
questions.simple: True, past 5 percent I mostly wait for a tighter trigger. I never squeeze the stop to fit the size.

reasons: stop width options are held (D-005)
rests on the owner's size-from-the-stop rule (A5, A3)
the wider-than-3% claim comes from our own examples

questions.q: Do you add to it?
choices: No, one entry, one stop
Yes, add half, better average
Add once volume dries up
No, but widen the stop
questions.why: No. One entry, full size, one stop. That's the whole trade. Parabolic runs go further than anyone thinks. Bracco never adds when he's down, and neither do we. Add here and a squeeze hits a bigger position with the same stop. That's how a 1R loss turns into a blow-up. Widening the stop isn't an escape either. It only moves your way.
questions.lesson_line: Averaging up a short turns a 1R loss into a blow-up.

wrong.Yes, add half, better average: A better average with a bigger position just means a bigger squeeze.
wrong.Add once volume dries up: No signal makes adding to a loser okay. One entry, one stop.
wrong.No, but widen the stop: The stop is the exit. It never moves wider.

questions.story: Your short is almost 1R against you, still under the high of the day. A buddy in chat says add more, the top's in.
questions.simple: No, we take one entry with one stop. Adding to a losing short is how a small loss becomes a big one.

reasons: rests on the owner's one-entry and stop rules (A5, A4)

questions.q: Bracco has a tell for when these climax moves tend to peak. Which days does he watch?
choices: Thu or Fri into monthly expiry
The first day of a new rally
A quiet week with no hype at all
Week one out of a long base
questions.answer: Thu or Fri into monthly expiry
questions.why: Thursdays and Fridays, especially into monthly options expiration. That's where Bracco sees a lot of these climaxes peak. Use it to get ready, not to get in. If a burst is building into expiry week, have it on your radar the night before, borrow checked. A Thursday into expiry with no burst, no gap and no crack is still nothing. You still short the VWAP break, whatever the day.
questions.lesson_line: Thursday or Friday into expiry is a cue, not a trigger.

wrong.A quiet week with no hype at all: No hype, no crowd to wear out. These tops come when everyone's piling in.
wrong.The first day of a new rally: Nothing is stretched on day one of a rally. Climaxes come at the end of a run.
wrong.Week one out of a long base: Week one out of a base is far too early. That's a breakout, not a climax.

questions.simple: Thursdays and Fridays into monthly options expiration. It's a cue that helps, never the trigger.

deeper.trap: Expiration week is a cue, not a trigger. A Thursday or Friday into expiration with no gap up, no crack and no burst is still not a trade. The cue only adds weight to a climax that already has everything else.

reasons: the context cues are the card's proposal (D-023 pending)
an options-calendar cue

questions.q: That short lost. What was the mistake?
choices: Shorted strength, no crack
None, any gap up is a climax
The stop over the high was tight
Too late, the open was the entry
questions.why: You shorted strength. The day closed 7.3% over its open, so it never cracked. One box isn't a burst either. A green close on a gap day means buyers held it all day. Shorting a green climax day won 23% of the time, and this one lost 4.5R on the next day's gap up. We short the VWAP break during the day, never the close. No crack, no trade.
questions.lesson_line: A green close with one box is strength. Don't short strength.

wrong.The stop over the high was tight: The stop wasn't the problem. The entry was: a green day with one box.
wrong.None, any gap up is a climax: A gap that closes green hasn't cracked. The gap sets it up, the crack triggers it.
wrong.Too late, the open was the entry: Nothing at the open on a climax day. The problem was shorting a day that never cracked.

questions.story: After a run, the last bar gaps up 2.2% and closes 7.3% over its open. Only one burst box is checked. You short the close anyway.
questions.simple: Shorting strength. It closed well over its open, so it never cracked, and one box isn't a burst.

reasons: figures come from our own scan

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Bracco: most climax points come at obvious ___ numbers.
questions.why: Round. Bracco: most of these climax points occur around very obvious, round numbers. Our card adds that a chart parabolic even on a log scale is the strong form. It is a cue, not a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Watch the big round numbers. Bracco sees many climaxes there.
questions.simple: Bracco says most climax points come at very obvious round numbers.

reasons: the log-scale form is the card's cue

questions.q: Where was the error?
choices: Calling a top on a young run
Placing the stop over the high
Not holding past the new high
Using the 9 EMA as the target
questions.answer: Calling a top on a young run
questions.why: Calling a top on a young run: shorting a stock fresh out of a base. Bracco: a very short lived trade if it set up. RGTI had only 2 up closes before a 3.9% gap, reached the 9 EMA on day 5 at 0.99R, then a new high on day 6 took the stop. The stop and the target did their jobs. The context was wrong.
questions.lesson_line: Right candle, wrong week. A stock just out of a base has fuel.

wrong.Not holding past the new high: Over the high you are wrong. Holding through it is the blow-up.
wrong.Placing the stop over the high: A few cents over the high is the rule. It did its job on day 6.
wrong.Using the 9 EMA as the target: The target was right and it was reached. The context was wrong.

questions.story: Fresh out of a base: two up days, then a 3.9% gap that closes red. You short 31.64, stop 34.44. Day 5 touches the 9 EMA at 0.99R; day 6 a new high takes the stop.
questions.simple: The error was shorting a stock fresh out of a base. It had fuel left, and a new high on day 6 hit the stop.

deeper.trap: The 9 EMA was reached at 0.99R, so the trade looks almost fine, and only 1.14R was ever available. That is the trap: a near-miss on the numbers hides a wrong setup. Right candle, wrong week.

reasons: figures come from our own scan

questions.q: Where should the short have been?
choices: At the VWAP break, after the turn
At the close, it's five stars
At the break of the day's low
Nowhere, five-star tops are traps
questions.answer: At the VWAP break, after the turn
questions.why: At the VWAP break, after the turn. That's our entry on every short: during the day, never at the close. Shorting the close put the stop 34.3% away, and it ran only 0.40R before a new high on day 10 took it. The VWAP break at 90.01 ran 1.16R before the same 107.90 stop. Better, but that stop is still way past the 5% I accept. On a climax this wild, I'd mostly wait for a tighter trigger or let it go.
questions.lesson_line: Grade the setup, then pick the entry. Never the close.

wrong.At the break of the day's low: That's Bracco's second entry. We take one, at the VWAP break.
wrong.At the close, it's five stars: Five stars grades the setup, not the entry. It doesn't fix a 34.3% stop.
wrong.Nowhere, five-star tops are traps: The four boxes were real. The entry at the close was the problem.

questions.story: A five-star climax, four of four boxes. The day closed at its low. Short the close at 80.33 and the stop goes to 107.90, 34.3% away.
questions.simple: At the VWAP break during the day. A short at the close put the stop 34.3 percent away.

deeper.counter: Five stars grades the setup, not the entry. SMCI's four of four boxes were real, and it was Bracco's own five-star example, yet the close-entry short lost. Grade and entry are two separate decisions.

reasons: numbers come from one dossier row read off our own bars (the examples are unreviewed)
stop width options are held (D-005)
fixed before

questions.q: Kullamagi wants a smaller cap up 300% to 1,000% or more before he calls it a parabolic short candidate.
questions.why: True. A stock up 50-100%+ in days or weeks if larger cap, or 300-1000%+ if smaller cap. Small caps need a far bigger run.
questions.lesson_line: The smaller the stock, the bigger the run it takes to exhaust.

questions.q: What rule capped the damage?
choices: The window and three tries a week
No rule; three losses is a mistake
The 2R gap ceiling
questions.answer: The window and three tries a week
questions.why: The 1 to 2 day window and the cap of 3 tries in a week. Bracco: 3 failed attempts over 2 sessions, no revenge trade, no averaging down. Then he dropped it.
questions.lesson_line: Three tries, no revenge, no adding. Then walk away.

wrong.No rule; three losses is a mistake: Three planned losses inside the window is the rule working. Revenge-shorting would be the mistake.
wrong.The 2R gap ceiling: No gap through the stop here. Each stop was taken in the session.

questions.story: Bracco shorted AGQ three times in two sessions and was stopped each time. He did not add and did not revenge trade.

questions.q: It's still under the 200-day. Can you short it?
choices: Yes, shorts under it are fine
Only if the 200-day points down
No, parabolic shorts need above
No, a gap up is strength
questions.answer: Yes, shorts under it are fine
questions.why: Yes. Under the 200-day is where we short. The exception runs the other way: above the 200-day, the parabolic short is the only short we take. So below the line this one needs no excuse. It still needs the setup: the burst, the gap, the crack under VWAP and a stop over the high of the day.
questions.lesson_line: Under the 200-day a short needs no excuse. Above it, only the parabolic one.

wrong.Only if the 200-day points down: The rule looks at where the stock sits, not which way the line points.
wrong.No, parabolic shorts need above: The exception lets a parabolic short sit above the line. It doesn't stop you shorting below it.
wrong.No, a gap up is strength: The gap is part of the setup. The 200-day only decides whether a short is allowed.

questions.story: A stock under its 200-day rips higher in a burst, then ends with a 6% gap up and a closing reversal.
questions.simple: Yes, shorts under the 200-day need no exception. You still need the gap, the crack and the stop.

deeper.trap: Under the 200-day doesn't make it parabolic. The line only decides whether a short is allowed at all. The burst, the gap and the VWAP trigger still have to be there.

reasons: one cited fact only (B26, h01) carries the key
rests on the owner's rulebook (B26)
the exception test above the line is held (D-040)
fixed before (the CAR example was removed)

questions.q: Short 48.50, stop 52.56. The stock gaps over the stop and the first 30-minute high is 53.40. How many R is the loss there?
questions.why: 1.21R. The 30-minute high minus the fill, over the stop minus the fill. Inside the 2R ceiling, so 53.40 is the new stop, not an exit.
questions.lesson_line: Measure the gap in R. Under 2R the 30-minute high is the stop; past it, you are out.

questions.q: Bracco: the climax day almost always shows the highest OPENING volume of the whole run.
questions.why: True. Opening volume rises over several days, with the climax day almost invariably showing the highest opening volume of the entire run. Range and volume expansion come first.
questions.lesson_line: The biggest open of the run is the crowd arriving. That is who you sell to.

questions.q: Red close, record volume, but no gap. Is it the climax-day short?
choices: No, it never gapped up
Yes, the red close is the crack
Yes, record volume is enough
No, a burst needs five up days
questions.why: No. No gap up, no climax-day short. The gap is the exhaustion, the last buyers paying up at the open. This day opened under the prior close, so that last rush never came. Bracco won't short without that gap-up, and neither do we. Record volume and a red close make it feel like a climax. Without the gap, it's just a red day.
questions.lesson_line: The gap is the exhaustion. No gap, just a red day.

wrong.Yes, the red close is the crack: The crack only counts after a gap up. No gap, nothing to crack.
wrong.Yes, record volume is enough: Volume adds weight to a climax that gapped. It doesn't replace the gap.
wrong.No, a burst needs five up days: A burst runs 3-5 days, so four is fine. The missing gap is the problem.

questions.story: A four-day burst. Day five opens under the prior close, runs up, then closes red on record volume.
questions.simple: No. It opened under the prior close, so there was no gap up, and without the gap there's no climax short.

deeper.trap: A red close on record volume feels like a climax. Don't let it talk you in. The gap up is the exhaustion, and without it the day is just a red day. Bracco won't short without that gap-up.

reasons: the gap is a required box by Bracco and the card, which other sources do not require
rests on the owner's burst definition (B26)

questions.q: It finally paid 2.95R at best. What's the lesson?
choices: Out of time, and the gap was weak
Hold five weeks, it paid 2.95R
A 2.8% gap is a strong signal
A close at the low means it falls fast
questions.answer: Out of time, and the gap was weak
questions.why: It ran out of time, and the gap was its weak point. A 2.8% gap passes, but it's small. 5% or more is the strong one. The bigger issue is time. This trade pays at the 9 EMA in a few sessions, or not at all. Here the 9 EMA took 8 sessions, and the stock chopped under its high for five weeks. 2.95R was the best point, not the plan. One slow winner doesn't make sitting in dead shorts a good habit.
questions.lesson_line: No 9 EMA in a few sessions, the climax is out of time.

wrong.Hold five weeks, it paid 2.95R: 2.95R was the best print, and the 9 EMA took 8 sessions. This trade isn't meant to sit that long.
wrong.A 2.8% gap is a strong signal: 5% or more is the strong gap. 2.8% was the weak spot.
wrong.A close at the low means it falls fast: A close at the low is no promise. This one still chopped under its high for five weeks.

questions.story: Four of four boxes and a close at the low of the day, but the gap was only 2.8%. You're short 502.85, stop 547.76. It chops under the high for five weeks.
questions.simple: It ran out of time. This trade pays at the 9 EMA in a few sessions, and the small gap was its weak spot.

deeper.trap: Don't take 2.95R as proof that holding works. It was the best point, and the 9 EMA took 8 sessions, with five weeks of chop under the high. One slow winner doesn't change how this trade pays: fast, or not at all.

reasons: the 3-session cover is the dossier's proposed rule (ps.time_limit), not yet the owner's
numbers come from one dossier row read off our own bars (the examples are unreviewed)
fixed before

questions.q: Bracco has a name for this. What is it, and how does he feel about it?
choices: Quick range breakdown, not a fan
The U-Turn, his favorite
A five-star climax, the best kind
Drawn-out range, he avoids it
questions.answer: Quick range breakdown, not a fan
questions.why: The Quick Opening Range Breakdown, and he's not a fan. The high comes on the first 5-minute candle, then the 2- or 5-minute opening range breaks. Bracco calls it less frequent and more challenging, and it needs caution. It often shows up on day 1 or 2 of the burst, too early in the move. The climax gap comes on day 3 to 5. So count the days before you trust a first-candle top.
questions.lesson_line: A first-candle top on day two is often not the top.

wrong.The U-Turn, his favorite: The U-Turn runs first and cracks 10 to 60 minutes in. This one topped on the first candle.
wrong.A five-star climax, the best kind: Day two of a burst is early. The climax gap comes on day 3 to 5.
wrong.Drawn-out range, he avoids it: That's a tight range for the first one to two hours. This topped on the very first candle.

questions.story: Day two of a burst. Today it gaps up, sets its high on the first 5-minute candle and breaks the opening range low.
questions.simple: The Quick Opening Range Breakdown. Bracco isn't fond of it, since it often comes too early in the run.

deeper.trap: Count the days before you trust a first-candle top. The climax gap comes on day 3 to 5 of the burst. On day 1 or 2, the same shape is often too early in the move.

reasons: one author's view (Bracco), cited from the post's own words
fixed before: the key said weakest and least liked, which the post does not say; it now says not fond

questions.q: Bracco: a frequent mistake is judging a stock by its percent gain alone and ignoring the chart's structure.
questions.why: True. Relying solely on a stock's percentage gain, overlooking its chart structure and formation, is the mistake he names. A linear run, however far it has gone, is not this setup.
questions.lesson_line: The number gets you looking. The shape gets you the trade.

questions.q: You're gapped way through your stop. What now?
choices: Out at once, past the 2R line
New stop 74.00, the 30-min high
Hold, it has to come back down
New stop 72.00, the open
questions.answer: Out at once, past the 2R line
questions.why: Out, right away. The gap rule gives the first 30 minutes a say, but with a ceiling: past 2R, you're out. The open at 72.00 is already 4R against your 60.00 entry and 63.00 stop. There's nothing to wait for. This is how this setup does real damage: a squeeze gaps over the stop for 4R to 5R losses. Take the hit and keep it from getting worse.
questions.lesson_line: The gap rule has a ceiling. Past 2R, you're out.

wrong.New stop 74.00, the 30-min high: The 30-minute high is the new stop only inside 2R. This is way past it.
wrong.Hold, it has to come back down: Nothing has to come back. A squeeze through your stop is how this trade does real damage.
wrong.New stop 72.00, the open: The open is never the stop. And past 2R there's no new stop. You're out.

questions.story: You shorted the crack at 60.00, stop 63.00. Overnight news hits. It opens at 72.00, and the first 30-minute high is 74.00.
questions.simple: Get out. The gap already took you past 2R, and past 2R in the first half hour, you leave.

deeper.trap: Nothing promises the stock comes back to the 9 EMA. The gap rule isn't a way to wait. It's a short window with a hard ceiling. Past 2R the plan is over.

reasons: rests on the owner's gap rule and its 2R ceiling (B20)
the key needs a loss worked out from the story

questions.q: Small gap. Does that kill the trade?
choices: No, it passes, just weaker
Yes, it needs 5% or more
Yes, small gaps show no exhaustion
No, gap size doesn't matter
questions.why: No. Any open over the prior close passes, and 1.7% does. It's just a weaker gap. 5% or more is the strong one. Weigh it against the rest of the chart. SCHW in 1999 had four boxes and three record-volume days, and it hit the 9 EMA the next session. The small gap was its weak point, not a deal breaker. That's a grading call, and it's judgment.
questions.lesson_line: Any gap up passes. A big gap grades higher.

wrong.Yes, it needs 5% or more: 5% or more is the stronger gap, not the minimum. Any gap up passes.
wrong.Yes, small gaps show no exhaustion: This one had four boxes and three record-volume days, and it hit the 9 EMA the next session.
wrong.No, gap size doesn't matter: It matters. A bigger gap grades higher. A small one passes but counts for less.

questions.simple: No, any gap up passes. A small one counts for less, but four boxes and record volume still carry it.

deeper.trap: Don't read weak as skip. SCHW's 1.7% gap was the weak point. Yet it had four boxes and three record-volume days, and it hit the 9 EMA the next session. One weak mark lowers the grade. It doesn't cancel the rest.

reasons: rests on the criteria card's grade rows (grading is discretionary, E50)
fixed before
the count of boxes needed is held (D-040)

questions.story: Four boxes and record volume, but the climax gap on the last bar is only 1.7%.

questions.q: Give me the plan: entry, stop, target.
choices: Market now, stop over high, 9 EMA
Short the open, 3% stop, 3R
Wait for the close, stop at the 9 EMA
Market now, stop at VWAP, 9 EMA
questions.answer: Market now, stop over high, 9 EMA
questions.why: Market now, stop just over the high of the day, cover at the daily 9 EMA. The VWAP break is the trigger, so you're in at market. The stop goes a few cents over the high, where the idea's proven wrong. The target is the 9 EMA, the magnet it snaps back to. BILI's daily stand-in was a short at 29.66, stop 31.81, and the 9 EMA came in 4 sessions. That stop was 7.2% away, past the 5% I accept. On a stop that wide I mostly wait for a tighter trigger.
questions.lesson_line: VWAP break in, stop over the high, out at the 9 EMA.

Yes, three tries are allowed

questions.why: No. Drop it. Each idea gets a 1 to 2 day window, and two failed triggers or the window passing ends it. You've got both. Three tries a week on one stock is the outer cap, not a license to keep swinging. I'd rather miss the move than get chopped up by one attempt after another. The first climax of a mania is often not the last. Wait for the next real one.

wrong.Yes, three tries are allowed: Three a week is the outer cap, not a target. Two failures ends the idea.
wrong.Yes, the window resets daily: The window counts from the climax. It doesn't reset each morning.
wrong.No, the stop was too tight: The stop was right, a few cents over the high. The window closing is why you drop it.

questions.story: The climax came Monday. Tuesday and Wednesday, both triggers failed and stopped you out. Thursday it cracks under VWAP again.
questions.simple: No, two failed tries and the window's closed. Chasing a third is how you get chopped up.

deeper.trap: The idea has a clock. A fresh crack on Thursday feels new, but it's the same run with two failed triggers behind it. Wait for the next climax, not a retry. Stamatoudis says the same: he'd rather miss the move than be chopped up by early attempts.

questions.q: Why does Bracco steer you away from a steady, linear ascent?

It always ends in a sharp gap down
It has too little volume to measure
It trades under the 200-day line

wrong.It always ends in a sharp gap down: A linear run has no reliable end. It can run on, and that is the point.
wrong.It has too little volume to measure: Volume can be measured on any run. The issue is the shape: steady, not accelerating.
wrong.It trades under the 200-day line: The 200-day is a separate test. This is about the shape of the run.
